Replay

Editor-first Replay authoring and canonical Scrapyard

2 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Ownership rulesDelivery sequenceCurrent status

Completed 2026-09-20; see delivery assessment.

Goal: make normal Godot scene composition the everyday presentation workflow around Replay's composed value simulation. Replay Scrapyard is the canonical worked example, alongside the untouched original game. This follows the completed bridge and its initial Scrapyard integration; it is not a new full-game parity campaign.

Ownership rules#

  • Editor scenes own visual hierarchy, authored assets, layout and presentation tuning. Scene-local scripts own cached children and animation clocks.
  • Gameplay modules own replayable state/rules. Authoring Resources become validated immutable values before runner admission. Node animation cannot commit damage.
  • Adapters choose predicted/observed/authority values and feed detached displays. They own view identity and session/recovery boundaries, not sprite animation.
  • Composition exists on both sides: typed state/modules for gameplay, reusable child scenes/scripts for presentation. No mandatory ECS or extra Replay-specific code generation.
  • Root transforms have one owner. Authored offsets/animation belong beneath that root. Views may run their normal Godot process lifecycle; framework frame hooks remain available for deliberately centralized/batched renderers.
  • Procedural arenas, trails and high-churn batches may remain procedural when their geometry/data is generated. Document those exceptions and their ownership.

Delivery sequence#

Gate Work Required evidence
E1 Typed scripted-scene binding and practical ownership contract Wrong script/invalid component rejection, ready/present/process/retire lifetime, native/WASM
E2 Authored enemy appearance and reusable telegraph component Scene-local enemy animation, no Session/World access; independent preview; real actor/feedback behavior and editor-authored changes
E3 Authored player scene composed with weapon/equipment views Detached display/cue inputs, child-owned visuals, preserved prediction/smoothing and fixed-seat semantics; down/respawn/equipment/camera checks
E4 Validated Resource authoring and gameplay composition recipe Scrapyard catalog bake with useful source errors, duplicate IDs/ranges rejected atomically; stock/hash and representative edits; documented composed gameplay components
E5 Canonical onboarding and editor workflow Scene map, responsibility map, F6 previews, extending an enemy/weapon/behavior; explicit procedural exceptions and multiplayer/recovery policy
E6 Integration and performance assessment Focused scene/native/WASM checks, host/client/observer agreement, recovery-sensitive scopes, representative measured costs without unfair old/new animation timing; preserve originals and model/wire contracts

Success means a developer can open an actor scene, edit its visual children or presentation settings, preview it independently, and connect it to replayable state through a small typed adapter. New gameplay behavior remains an explicit state/rule change with a documented authoring/baking path. Scrapyard should teach that distinction through runnable code, not only prose.

Current status#

E1–E6 complete. The canonical guide reflects the migrated scenes, typed adapters, Resource baking, procedural exceptions and measured/validated support envelope.
